An EDR alert shows a third-party service binary (running as NETWORK SERVICE) creating an ALPC port via NtCreatePort / AlpcCreatePort, registering a security descriptor that allows WORLD or specific SIDs to connect. A high-privileged process (winlogon.exe, LUID 0x3e7) then connects to that port. The service thread subsequently invokes AlpcImpersonateClient (or the legacy NtImpersonateClientOfPort), after which its effective token SID becomes SYSTEM and it enables SeDebugPrivilege. No named-pipe creation or ImpersonateNamedPipeClient calls are present. What kernel mechanism allowed the token transfer, why would a privileged system process connect to an untrusted third-party ALPC port, and what telemetry gaps exist for this vector compared to classic named-pipe impersonation?

<reasoning>The presence of an ALPC Port object created by a third-party NETWORK SERVICE binary, followed by an inbound connection from a SYSTEM LUID process such as winlogon.exe, is the first decisive anomaly. ALPC connection requests are mediated by the kernel object manager; the server thread can then invoke AlpcImpersonateClient (or the legacy NtImpersonateClientOfPort) which causes the LPC subsystem to replace the server thread token pointer with a reference to the client token captured at message receipt time, subject to the SeTokenCanImpersonate checks. Because the service binary is not a documented Windows broker and the port security descriptor was set permissively, a high-privileged process would only connect if it had been tricked through COM endpoint registration, an RPC interface collision, or another coercion path that resolved the port name or GUID. The immediate enable of SeDebugPrivilege on the resulting thread token proves both that the impersonation level was at least Impersonation and that the stolen token carried powerful privileges. Legitimate ALPC servers receiving SYSTEM connections are restricted to a small set of Microsoft-signed core components whose ports are registered in well-known locations; the absence of any such registration or binary signature match eliminates every benign explanation. The remaining hypothesis is deliberate ALPC token impersonation used for privilege escalation or to obtain a high-integrity context for further operations (T1134.001 combined with T1068 or T1557.001). This vector is stealthier than named-pipe impersonation because it leaves no pipe name or EID 17/18 artifacts and the coercion surface is the ALPC/RPC namespace rather than the filesystem.</reasoning>
<answer>{"vector": "ALPC port creation by untrusted binary + AlpcImpersonateClient after high-priv connection", "kernel_mechanism": "AlpcCreatePort + security descriptor set + AlpcConnectPort from client + AlpcImpersonateClient swaps thread token to captured client context", "why_priv_client_connected": "Coercion via planted COM endpoint or RPC port name collision targeting winlogon/lsass", "evidence_of_success": "SeDebugPrivilege (or other high priv) enabled on thread token immediately after impersonation call; no named-pipe activity", "mitre_techniques": ["T1134.001", "T1068", "T1557.001"], "telemetry_gaps": "No Sysmon 17/18; Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-Alpc ETW low volume or disabled; relies on object creation + privilege enable correlation", "recommended_hunts": ["Non-Microsoft image creates ALPC Port object with DACL allowing untrusted SIDs", "ALPC connection event (if available) or subsequent handle open from SYSTEM process to third-party service, followed by NtAdjustPrivilegesToken enabling SeDebug/SeTcb", "Process creation or OpenProcess calls under the impersonated SYSTEM SID from the service binary"], "risk_assessment": "High - powerful stealth token relay primitive that defeats pipe-centric detection rules"}</answer>

Sysmon and Kernel-Process ETW show a suspicious remote memory write (WriteProcessMemory + PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE allocation) into explorer.exe from a low-integrity malware process, followed by anomalous API calls and network beacon from the explorer process, but there is zero evidence of new thread creation (no ThreadStart/ThreadStop events) and no obvious SetThreadContext or CreateRemoteThread. The target thread in explorer was a pre-existing GUI thread in an alertable state. What injection technique is in use, why did it evade the standard thread-creation telemetry, and what additional ETW provider or behavioral signal closes this detection gap?

<reasoning>The complete absence of any Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-Process ThreadStart event for the target process after the observed remote memory write immediately eliminates every injection technique that allocates a new thread (CreateRemoteThread, RtlCreateUserThread, NtCreateThreadEx). The only execution primitive that can introduce attacker code into an already-running thread without creating a new ETHREAD object is delivery of a user APC to a thread that is currently in an alertable wait state. Explorer.exe and similar GUI or RPC threads spend the majority of their lifetime inside GetMessage or WaitForMultipleObjectsEx with the fAlertable flag set, making them ideal targets. The attacker performs WriteProcessMemory (or NtWriteVirtualMemory) + VirtualProtectEx to place shellcode in executable memory inside the target, obtains a handle to a specific TID that is alertable, and calls NtQueueApcThreadEx (or the legacy variant) to queue an APC whose NormalRoutine points at the shellcode. When the thread next enters user mode after its wait completes, the kernel APC dispatcher executes the routine in the target thread context. Default ETW configurations do not emit high-fidelity APC queuing or delivery events for user APCs; the relevant events exist only in the Microsoft-Windows-Threat-Intelligence provider, which is frequently disabled in production because of the volume of injection-related telemetry it generates. Direct syscall invocation further bypasses any ntdll-level hooking. The combination of cross-process executable memory modification + execution inside a pre-existing thread with zero new thread telemetry and no SetThreadContext activity is therefore diagnostic of T1055.004 APC Injection. Legitimate cross-process APC usage is extremely rare outside of debuggers and specific COM/DCOM scenarios, and those cases do not involve RWX allocations from low-integrity sources.</reasoning>
<answer>{"injection_technique": "User APC queued to existing alertable thread via NtQueueApcThreadEx after remote memory write", "etw_blind_spot": "No new ETHREAD allocation so no Kernel-Process ThreadStart/ThreadStop; user APC queuing events absent from default providers and only present (optionally) in Microsoft-Windows-Threat-Intelligence", "why_target_thread_suitable": "GUI/RPC threads in explorer.exe, svchost, etc. are frequently alertable (fAlertable=TRUE in kernel wait)", "mitre_techniques": ["T1055.004", "T1055.001"], "closing_the_gap": "Enable Threat-Intelligence ETW where performance allows; implement behavioral detection correlating remote WriteProcessMemory + NtProtectVirtualMemory to executable + NtQueueApcThreadEx on the same process handle within a short temporal window; post-execution stack inspection via GetThreadContext on suspicious threads", "recommended_hunts": ["Process performing WriteProcessMemory to remote process followed by handle to a specific thread in that process and a QueueApc syscall, with no subsequent ThreadStart events", "Anomalous APC execution manifested as execution of code at non-image-backed addresses in a thread whose creation predates the write"], "risk_assessment": "High for stealth - widely used in modern loaders because it evades the most common thread-creation detection rules"}</answer>

After initial compromise, a medium-integrity process suddenly calls LogonUserW specifying a domain account and LOGON32_PROVIDER_WINNT50, then passes the resulting token to CreateProcessWithTokenW to spawn a new process as that domain admin. The original process token never listed SeTcbPrivilege or SeCreateTokenPrivilege. The new logon appears in the security event log as a type 3 or 9 logon from an unexpected source. How exactly did the attacker construct a usable token for an arbitrary principal, and what kernel and LSA artifacts are the smoking gun?

<reasoning>The sudden ability of a previously medium-integrity process to call LogonUserW (or LsaLogonUser) for an arbitrary domain account and then feed the resulting handle to CreateProcessWithTokenW is only possible after the attacker has obtained a token containing SeTcbPrivilege. SeTcb (Act as part of the operating system) is not granted to normal user or service tokens; it is present on the primary tokens of winlogon.exe, lsass.exe, the SCM, and a handful of other core SYSTEM processes. The attacker therefore first had to acquire a usable copy of one of those tokens via prior impersonation, duplication from a handle leak, or a UAC bypass that produced a richer token. Once in possession of a primary token carrying SeTcb, DuplicateTokenEx with the appropriate access mask yields a duplicate that still contains the privilege. With SeTcb enabled, LogonUser can request a fresh logon session from the LSA (bypassing the normal interactive logon path through winlogon), and the resulting token can be passed directly to CreateProcessWithTokenW. The forensic artifacts are a new logon session (distinct TokenLogonSid) whose origin LUID and authentication package do not correspond to a legitimate interactive, network, or service logon initiated by the authentication stack, plus the source process performing the LogonUser call being unrelated to any known logon broker. No benign code path allows an arbitrary medium-integrity process to mint tokens for domain principals; this sequence is post-exploitation token forgery tradecraft (T1134.003, T1134.005) used to spawn processes under stolen or fabricated identities for lateral movement or persistence.</reasoning>
<answer>{"escalation_primitive": "Obtain SeTcb-bearing token via prior theft or impersonation, duplicate to primary, enable, then LogonUser + CreateProcessWithTokenW", "kernel_lsa_requirements": "SeTcbPrivilege (and SeCreateTokenPrivilege for direct NtCreateToken) must be present and enabled on the calling token", "smoking_gun_artifacts": "New logon session created from non-broker process; TokenOrigin or TokenLogonSid does not match expected authentication paths; LogonUser call from compromised medium process", "mitre_techniques": ["T1134.003", "T1134.005", "T1557.002"], "recommended_detection": ["Logon events (4624) with Logon Type 3/9/10 originating from processes other than winlogon.exe, logonui.exe, or lsass.exe", "Process calling LogonUser or LsaLogonUser that is not a documented authentication component", "CreateProcessWithTokenW calls where the source token was not acquired through standard elevation or delegation APIs"], "risk_assessment": "Very High - allows the attacker to operate as any principal for which they can authenticate, completely bypassing the original compromised identity"}</answer>

A signed but vulnerable kernel driver was loaded, after which several expected ETW events (ProcessStart, LoadImage, Registry) for subsequent activity stopped firing for a specific protected process (PPL). Later analysis with a kernel debugger shows that entries in the Psp*NotifyRoutine arrays have been zeroed or redirected, and the ETW registration for Microsoft-Windows-Threat-Intelligence has been tampered. What is the precise tradecraft the attacker used to suppress this telemetry, and how can a defender detect the tampering itself rather than relying on the now-absent events?

<reasoning>The sudden and selective disappearance of ProcessStart, LoadImage, and ThreadStart events for activity performed by or against a specific protected process (PPL) after a vulnerable kernel driver was loaded points directly to tampering with the kernel notification callback arrays. The arrays PspCreateProcessNotifyRoutine, PspLoadImageNotifyRoutine, and PspCreateThreadNotifyRoutine are fixed-size tables of function pointers maintained by the kernel; each registered driver or component occupies a slot. With arbitrary kernel read/write obtained through the vulnerable driver, the attacker can locate these arrays (via pattern scanning or by walking the unexported Psp* globals) and zero the relevant slots or replace the callbacks with stubs that simply return. This prevents the normal callback invocation that would have generated the corresponding ETW events and would have allowed EDR callbacks to inspect the new process or image. The same driver can also unregister or filter ETW providers such as Microsoft-Windows-Threat-Intelligence. Because the notify routines execute early in process creation (before PPL protection flags are fully applied in some code paths), the tampering allows creation and injection into protected processes that would otherwise be blocked or heavily logged. The decisive detection signal is not the missing events themselves (which could be explained by filtering or provider disable) but the post-driver-load mismatch in the number and addresses of registered callbacks when compared against a known-good baseline, or direct observation of writes to the memory pages containing the notify routine tables. This is rootkit-style kernel tampering (T1014) used in conjunction with process injection or protected process abuse (T1055, T1547.006).</reasoning>
<answer>{"tampering_target": "Kernel notification callback arrays (PspCreateProcessNotifyRoutine et al.) and ETW provider registration via vulnerable signed driver", "effect": "Prevents callback invocation for attacker-created processes/images/threads; suppresses ETW events for PPL and injection activity", "why_it_works_on_ppl": "Callbacks run before or during early initialization; zeroing the slot removes the check that would have seen the new protected process", "detection_of_tampering": "Live kernel forensics (!processcallbacks, !devobj, callback enumeration tools) showing unexpected zeroed or altered entries after specific driver load; memory integrity monitoring or driver block list hits on the loaded vulnerable binary; anomalous kernel writes from user-mode process to known notify routine structures", "mitre_techniques": ["T1014", "T1547.006", "T1055"], "recommended_defense": "Block or heavily monitor load of known vulnerable drivers (Microsoft recommended driver block list); implement kernel callback integrity checks at boot and periodically; enable full Threat-Intelligence ETW and correlate with driver load events; use HVCI / Memory Integrity where possible to raise the bar for kernel R/W", "risk_assessment": "Critical - defeats entire classes of callback and ETW-based detection until the tampering itself is discovered"}</answer>

A kernel-level EDR component and Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-Process ETW provider logged a ProcessStart event for PID 4812, a process image named "spoolsv.exe" with a command line containing a suspicious DLL path in a user-writable directory and a parent process that was a low-integrity dropper. Network and file telemetry continued to be attributed to PID 4812 for the next 40 minutes (C2 beacons, writes to HKCU Run key, lateral SMB connections). However, every attempt to enumerate running processes via standard APIs (CreateToolhelp32Snapshot, EnumProcesses, WMI Win32_Process, or even direct NtQuerySystemInformation) returns no entry for PID 4812. Tasklist, Get-Process, and the EDR process tree view also omit it completely. A live kernel memory dump shows the EPROCESS structure for 4812 is allocated and its handle table and other fields are populated and consistent with a running process, but the Flink and Blink pointers in its ActiveProcessLinks have been overwritten to point back to itself, removing it from the PsActiveProcessHead circular doubly-linked list. No ProcessStop or ProcessTerminate ETW event was ever generated for this PID. What precise kernel data structure manipulation was performed, at what point in the process lifecycle, which standard detection telemetry paths does it defeat, and what alternative signals would allow a defender to detect and attribute activity to such a hidden process?

<reasoning>The continued attribution of malicious post-compromise activity (C2, registry persistence, lateral movement) to PID 4812 combined with the complete absence of that PID from every process enumeration API and list-walking mechanism is the central anomaly. A benign explanation would require either that the process had already exited (which would produce a ProcessStop event and cease all attributed activity) or that the initial ProcessStart event was fabricated by user-mode code. Both are impossible: the ETW event originated from the Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-Process provider which is emitted by the kernel itself during PspCreateProcess and PspInsertProcess, and the subsequent IO and network operations attributed to the PID prove the process is still executing code and owning handles. The kernel debugger confirmation of a live EPROCESS whose only defect is a self-referential ActiveProcessLinks entry tells us the unlink happened after the process was inserted into the global list and after the creation notification callbacks (PspCreateProcessNotifyRoutine) had already executed and emitted the ETW record. Therefore the attacker must have obtained arbitrary kernel read/write (via a previously loaded vulnerable signed driver or an earlier exploit) and used it to locate the EPROCESS for the newly created PID (by PID hash table or by walking the list once and caching the pointer) and then atomically overwrote the Flink and Blink fields to excise the entry from the circular list while leaving every other field intact. This defeats every detection and response component that discovers processes exclusively by walking PsActiveProcessHead or by calling the documented system information classes that ultimately rely on that same list. Because the process creation path completed normally, the malware can continue to allocate memory, load images, open handles, and perform all normal operations; only its visibility is removed. Hypotheses such as container isolation or Pico process artifacts are eliminated because a real EPROCESS with a full handle table and committed address space exists in the dump. The missing ProcessStop is explained by the fact that the malware never calls the exit path; it simply continues running while hidden. This is textbook DKOM process hiding performed after the notification window has closed.</reasoning><answer>{"technique":"DKOM unlink of EPROCESS.ActiveProcessLinks from PsActiveProcessHead after creation notifications and ETW emission","lifecycle_point":"Immediately after PspInsertProcess and PspCreateProcessNotifyRoutine callbacks have fired","blind_spots":"ZwQuerySystemInformation(SystemProcessInformation), CreateToolhelp32Snapshot, WMI Win32_Process queries, most EDR user-mode and some kernel process tree builders that walk the global list, many rootkit detection heuristics","why_no_stop_event":"The process object was never terminated or instructed to exit; the malware continues executing normally with intact handle table and address space","mitre_techniques":["T1014","T1055","T1564.001"],"telemetry_gaps":"All list-based process discovery is blind to the process; only the initial ETW ProcessStart plus any subsequent behavioral telemetry (file, registry, network) explicitly attributed to the PID by the kernel scheduler or object manager can reveal its existence","recommended_hunts":["Correlate every Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-Process ProcessStart event against live process snapshots taken minutes later; flag any PID that performed attributed activity (file writes, reg sets, TCP connections) but is absent from all enumeration APIs and has no ProcessStop event","Monitor for PIDs that appear in ETW ThreadStart, ImageLoad, or Registry events but are unreachable via OpenProcess with PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION or via standard list APIs","Periodic kernel-assisted EPROCESS pool scanning or cross-check of the PID hash table (PspCidTable) against the ActiveProcess list to surface orphaned but live process objects"],"risk_assessment":"Critical - provides near-complete stealth against the majority of process-discovery-based detection, forensics, and response tooling while preserving full process functionality and ability to perform malicious actions"}</answer>

An EDR agent on a domain-joined workstation reports no Sysmon Event ID 10 (ProcessAccess) or equivalent handle-open telemetry when a low-privileged service binary (running as NETWORK SERVICE) suddenly opens lsass.exe and several other high-privilege processes with PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION | PROCESS_VM_READ access rights. The only preceding event is the load of a signed but known-vulnerable third-party kernel driver. Subsequent token duplication succeeds and a new process appears running as SYSTEM. A kernel debugger attached later shows that the ObTypeList for PsProcessType and PsThreadType has had its registered callback entries (from ObRegisterCallbacks) zeroed or replaced with no-op stubs for the specific altitude used by the EDR. What object-manager callback mechanism was disabled, why did the EDR's primary handle-acquisition signal disappear while the process continued to run, and which secondary telemetry source (ETW, handle table enumeration, or object directory walk) can still reveal the tampering?

<reasoning>The complete and selective absence of any ProcessAccess or Ob-callback-derived event for the acquisition of handles to lsass.exe and winlogon.exe immediately rules out every normal OpenProcess path that would have triggered the EDR's registered ObPreOperationCallback and ObPostOperationCallback routines. The Windows Object Manager invokes these callbacks for every successful handle creation on monitored object types (Process, Thread, Token, Desktop, etc.) unless the callback list for that _OBJECT_TYPE has been deliberately modified. Because a vulnerable kernel driver was loaded moments earlier, the attacker obtained arbitrary kernel read/write, located the OB_TYPE_OBJECT_TYPE structures (via the global ObTypeDirectory or by walking type indices), and unlinked or zeroed the specific callback entry whose altitude and cookie matched the EDR's registration. This leaves the actual handle table entry created in the target process's handle table but generates zero notification to user-mode components. Benign explanations such as a legitimate driver unloading its callbacks or the EDR itself deregistering are eliminated: the EDR agent process remains running, continues to emit other telemetry (process creation, image loads), and no corresponding driver unload or Cm callback deregistration events exist. The subsequent successful token theft from lsass using the newly opened handles confirms that the OpenProcess call truly succeeded with the requested access mask. This is the classic ObRegisterCallbacks tampering technique (frequently paired with Bring-Your-Own-Vulnerable-Driver) used for T1003.001 and T1055. The smoking-gun mismatch is between the live kernel handle table (visible via kernel enumeration or !handle) and the total lack of Ob callback events. Detection therefore requires either periodic integrity validation of the callback lists from a more privileged vantage point (hypervisor or early-boot driver), cross-correlation with ETW Threat Intelligence events that sometimes take a parallel path, or direct auditing of the object directory and registered altitudes.</reasoning>
<answer>{"vector": "ObRegisterCallbacks tampering via vulnerable driver to suppress handle-open notifications for credential access and injection", "kernel_mechanism": "Locate OB_TYPE_OBJECT_TYPE for Process/Thread via ObTypeDirectory or type index, walk CallbackList head, unlink or replace the EDR's altitude-specific entry with a stub", "telemetry_observed": "Vulnerable driver load (Sysmon 6 or ETW) + subsequent successful OpenProcess against lsass without any ProcessAccess/Ob events + token duplication + new SYSTEM process", "telemetry_absent": "Sysmon EID 10, EDR ObPre/PostOperationCallback events for all sensitive Process/Thread handle opens", "why_benign_unlikely": "EDR agent still running and emitting other events; no driver unload for the EDR altitude; exact temporal correlation with vulnerable driver load; successful privileged operations follow", "mitre_techniques": ["T1003.001", "T1055", "T1543.003"], "telemetry_gaps": "ObRegisterCallbacks are the primary mechanism for most EDRs to receive notifications on handle opens; once the callback node is removed from the list, no user-mode notification is delivered for that object type", "recommended_hunts": ["Vulnerable or unsigned driver load events immediately followed by a sharp drop to zero ProcessAccess events targeting lsass.exe, winlogon.exe, or services.exe from non-standard processes", "Periodic kernel callback list enumeration (altitude, cookie, pre/post routine addresses) compared against a known-good baseline of EDR registrations", "Use of cross-view process enumeration (ETW ProcessStart + handle table scan via NtQuerySystemInformation) that reveals handles the Ob layer never reported"], "risk_assessment": "Critical - silently defeats the core handle-acquisition detection surface used by nearly all modern EDR products for LSASS access and process injection"}</answer>

The EDR console on a cluster of high-value domain controllers stops receiving new process creation, image load, and registry change events approximately 90 seconds after a signed but vulnerable printer driver is loaded by a low-privileged service. Endpoint analysis shows that the real-time ETW trace session (named "EDRKernelTrace" with specific provider GUIDs) has been stopped via EVENT_TRACE_CONTROL_STOP. The call to ControlTraceW originated from the same service binary that loaded the driver. No ETW event documenting the session stop itself appears in the Application or System logs because the attacker targeted the logger object directly from kernel mode. Subsequent attacker activity (credential dumping, lateral movement) occurs with zero corresponding EDR alerts. How did the attacker locate and terminate the EDR's specific ETW session without triggering session-control telemetry, and what alternative kernel or user-mode artifact can a defender rely on to detect deliberate creation of this ETW blind spot?

<reasoning>The sudden and complete cessation of process, image, and registry ETW events for an entire class of high-value systems, occurring immediately after a vulnerable driver load, cannot be explained by normal session expiration or resource pressure. Real-time ETW sessions used by EDR agents are created with WNODE_FLAG_TRACED or EVENT_TRACE_REAL_TIME_MODE and are referenced by a TRACEHANDLE obtained from StartTraceW. The attacker, having obtained kernel read/write through the vulnerable driver, either walked the global EtwpLoggerContext array (or the TRACEHANDLE-to-LOGGER structure mapping) to obtain the correct logger ID for the EDR session, or used the user-mode ControlTraceW path with the session name after the driver facilitated the required privilege. Issuing EVENT_TRACE_CONTROL_STOP on that handle causes the kernel to stop delivering buffers to the registered consumers and ultimately tears down the session. Because the stop was performed at the correct logger level, many ETW infrastructure events that would normally be generated for session manipulation are suppressed or routed only to the now-disabled session. Benign explanations (accidental stop by an admin tool, session timeout, or EDR self-update) are ruled out by the precise timing with the driver load, the absence of any corresponding service stop or configuration change in the EDR agent, and the fact that only the EDR-relevant providers were affected while other ETW sessions (Security log, Application log) continued. The technique therefore constitutes a deliberate ETW real-time session termination attack that creates a broad kernel telemetry blind spot (T1055.012 or T1562.002). The surviving artifacts are the missing session handle in the Etwp data structures, any lingering .etl file handles, and the sudden absence of events that should have been produced by the now-unmonitored activity.</reasoning>

A high-fidelity EDR that registers with the Microsoft-Windows-Threat-Intelligence ETW provider (GUID 22FB2CD6-0E7B-422B-A0E1-22D166F4C4A6) suddenly loses all visibility into process creation, image loads, thread creation, and driver loads performed by or against a specific set of high-value processes on several servers. The classic PspCreateProcessNotifyRoutine, PspLoadImageNotifyRoutine, and PspCreateThreadNotifyRoutine arrays remain intact (a secondary EDR using only legacy callbacks still receives some events). Kernel analysis shows that the ETW provider registration for Threat-Intelligence has been unregistered or its internal callback dispatch table entry has been zeroed. What is the difference between the ETW Threat Intelligence provider and the legacy Ps*NotifyRoutine arrays, why is the ETW-TI channel especially valuable for attackers to blind, and what kernel structures or registration APIs allow a defender to detect tampering with this specific provider?

<reasoning>The selective loss of rich kernel telemetry (process, thread, image, driver events with extended context such as command lines, full image paths, and caller process information) while the legacy Psp*NotifyRoutine arrays are untouched indicates targeted tampering with the Microsoft-Windows-Threat-Intelligence ETW provider rather than generic callback-array zeroing. The ETW-TI provider is implemented as a dedicated kernel ETW provider that many modern EDRs register for at load time; it receives notifications through a separate path (EtwpTraceKernelEvent or the dedicated Threat Intelligence instrumentation) that often includes more contextual data and is used for high-fidelity detections that the older notify routine callbacks cannot provide. Because the provider is registered via EtwRegister or the internal equivalent, and its dispatch is maintained in the ETW provider table (not the fixed-size Psp arrays), an attacker with kernel R/W can locate the provider's registration block by GUID and either call the unregistration path or zero the relevant function pointer in the provider's callback list. This creates a blind spot specifically for the rich events that the EDR relies on for its most precise rules, while leaving the legacy callbacks (used by Sysmon or older sensors) partially functional.
